Memorandum
TO:      Public Utility Commission of Texas

FROM: Jeff McDonald
         Michael Reinisch

DATE:    April 7, 2026

RE:      IMM Commentary on the Large Load Demand Management Service P-58482


We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the initial set of questions the PUC published to
structure the Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS) under the rulemaking
organized in Project 58482. The LLDMS has the potential to be an impactful tool for ERCOT to
procure significant demand reductions in response to high-risk conditions that materially threaten
the reliability of the ERCOT grid. We organize our comments into general comments first and
specific responses to the PUC’s questions next. We finish with a standalone executive summary.

A.    General Comments

In these comments, we outline several market design principles that we recommend the
Commission consider in developing the Large Load Demand Management Service.

First, to maximize the reliability value of the service while minimizing unnecessary cost to load,
the LLDMS should be designed as a targeted reliability tool whose procurement quantity and
budget can be tailored to the severity of an extreme event. A fixed seasonal budget adopted
primarily for administrative simplicity risks materially misaligning costs and benefits. In seasons
where no extreme events occur, a fixed budget may be expended without providing any
reliability value. The LLDMS should avoid replicating the structural limitations of the
Emergency Response Service by instead allowing procurement levels to reflect short-term
reliability needs.

Second, the LLDMS should be available for deployment during any extreme event that presents
a material risk of firm load shed, regardless of whether the event is weather-driven. When
forecasting supply and demand conditions, ERCOT should apply a stochastic risk methodology
that produces a profile of hourly probabilities of load shed for the anticipated event. The
magnitude of that risk should directly inform the procurement target and associated budget,
ensuring that the service is deployed in proportion to the reliability threat it is intended to
mitigate.


PUBLIC                                                                   © 2026 Potomac Economics
                              IMM Comments on the Large Load Demand Management Service P-58482
                                                                                 April 7, 2026



Third, ERCOT should evaluate the characteristics of different large load types to better
understand the budget necessary to procure a given quantity of demand reductions during an
extreme event. Empirical analysis of observed curtailment behavior by load type will be critical
to setting budgets that are sufficient to achieve reliability objectives without over-procurement.

Beyond these foundational principles, many of the most consequential design decisions will
depend on technical implementation details. To that end, we recommend that the Commission
host a workshop to further explore the following questions:

     •    What level of hourly probabilities of load shed during an event should qualify as
          sufficiently extreme to warrant deployment of the LLDMS?

     •    What risk methodology should ERCOT use to forecast hourly probabilities of load shed
          in advance of an extreme event?

     •    How should baselines be established, and at what point does baseline variability become
          too great for a load to participate?

     •    What threshold should be used to determine whether a load is price responsive for
          purposes of eligibility?

     •    What should a regular process for classifying loads as price responsive look like?

These questions require a careful balance between rigorous analytical inputs and stakeholder
judgment to arrive at reasonable and durable parameters for the new service. Given the
unprecedented load growth forecasted for the ERCOT region, we anticipate that a substantial
number of large loads will be technically eligible to participate in the LLDMS. Against that
backdrop, eligibility criteria should be designed to ensure that participation is limited to loads
capable of delivering clear incremental reliability value. Accordingly, we recommend that the
Commission adopt a robust set of qualification requirements, particularly with respect to the
establishment of reliable performance baselines and the determination of whether a load is price
responsive.

B.       Specific Comments to PUC Questions

         1.   Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a
              seasonal service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and
              why?

Option 1 is better aligned with market and reliability outcomes. Extreme weather events and
similar events that may materially stress system reliability are forecastable based on weather
data, scheduled outages, transmission limitations, fuel supply constraints, and other factors.
Accordingly, Option 1 allows ERCOT to set a budget based on the severity of an extreme event
based on a value that is rooted in the hourly probability of load shed throughout the duration of
the event.


PUBLIC                                         2
                            IMM Comments on the Large Load Demand Management Service P-58482
                                                                               April 7, 2026



Conversely, Option 2 would impose the same adverse effects and shortcomings as the
Emergency Response Service (ERS). Because the seasonal budget is set in advance, it cannot
reflect the true likelihood of extreme weather. In seasons with no qualifying events, the cost to
load yields no reliability value, while in seasons with multiple events, the budget may be
materially strained. Option 1, on the other hand, is only limited by the accuracy of the short-term
forecast that informs the budget, procured capacity, and offer price cap for an upcoming event.

      2.    PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop a
            reliability service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition.
            PURA § 39.170(b)(1) states the rules governing the new service must specify the
            periods when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during
            extreme weather events.

       a. Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances other than
          extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

We interpret PURA § 39.170(b) to require the LLDMS to be deployed during anticipated
emergency conditions and that while extreme weather events must be included and considered in
that definition, PURA does not limit the LLDMS to just extreme weather events.

ERCOT should deploy the LLDMS in any circumstance, including but not limited to extreme
weather events, where the forecast for the event period predicts a material hourly probability of
load shed. Effectively, our proposed definition would mirror the PUC’s definition for “Loss of
Load Event” in 16 TAC 25.508(a)(2) but with a defined hourly probability of load shed
threshold for a given extreme event period. At this time, we do not have a specific
recommendation for an hourly probability of load shed threshold and recommend that a
workshop be held to discuss it, but we do note that a winter storm like Winter Storm Fern would
not qualify as an extreme weather event.

       b. Should the commission define "extreme weather event" and, if so, how should it be
          defined?

The term “extreme weather event” should similarly be defined as a weather event during any
season for which a material hourly probability of load shed can be forecasted.

      3.    PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must prohibit
            participation by any large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale
            price of electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that otherwise participates in a
            different reliability or ancillary service. PURA § 37.0561(e)-which allows ERCOT to
            direct a large load customer with onsite backup generation to either curtail its load
            or deploy its backup generation under certain circumstances-states that a large load
            customer with onsite backup generation may participate in a service authorized by
            PURA § 39.170(b).


PUBLIC                                       3
                             IMM Comments on the Large Load Demand Management Service P-58482
                                                                                April 7, 2026



       a. What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load customer
          24 hours to ramp down safely?

No comments.

       b. What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any, should apply
          to participation in the new service?

Loads with highly variable operating profiles for which a reliable performance baseline cannot
be established should be excluded from participation in the LLDMS. If ERCOT is unable to
establish a defensible baseline for a participating load, compensation under the service may
produce unintended outcomes. It may result in no incremental reliability benefit if the baseline is
set materially above the load’s typical operating behavior, or it may impose an unexpectedly
severe and operationally disruptive curtailment obligation if the baseline is set too low.

That said, we would support the use of seasonal baselines in circumstances where a load’s
operating profile varies materially throughout the year and where a single annual baseline cannot
accurately reflect expected behavior. If a significant number of loads fall into this category, and
ERCOT can reliably establish baselines on a seasonal basis, a seasonal approach may improve
accuracy while preserving reliability value.

       c. Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as four
          coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude participation in the new
          service?

Yes. Loads that are responsive to 4CP are capable of responding to price. A load that participates
in 4CP response arguably has demonstrated (1) their capability to curtail significantly for the few
hours where it predicts that a peak load interval takes place and (2) their ability to do so
repeatedly throughout a season and during peak load conditions.

It is also important to consider the level of price that typically triggers a curtailment decision.
During the last several years, ERCOT has experienced very few intervals with true shortage
pricing at levels high enough, such as several thousand dollars per MWh, to motivate
discretionary curtailment. Because these conditions have been rare, it is difficult to establish a
reliable and consistent baseline for loads that would only respond under extreme price
conditions.

Excluding 4CP‑responsive loads from the LLDMS therefore has an additional benefit. It reduces
incentives for loads to engage in 4CP‑motivated operational changes in the future. This benefit
may ultimately depend on the cost allocation changes that emerge from Project 58484 and
whether that new framework sufficiently reduces incentives for 4CP gaming on its own.

       d. Should the commission define "curtailment in response to wholesale price of
          electricity" and, if so, how should it be defined?




PUBLIC                                        4
                             IMM Comments on the Large Load Demand Management Service P-58482
                                                                                April 7, 2026



As discussed above, the LLDMS is intended to be deployed only during extreme events where
ERCOT can forecast a material risk of firm load shed. Those conditions are typically associated
with severe system scarcity and wholesale energy prices that rise into the thousands of dollars
per MWh.

Accordingly, the definition of “curtailment in response to wholesale price of electricity” should
be calibrated to distinguish between discretionary economic behavior and reliability‑driven
response under high‑risk conditions. A definition that captures curtailment at price levels where,
e.g., cryptocurrency mines, routinely respond would risk excluding resources that provide no
incremental reliability value during extreme events.

When studying which loads should be disqualified from providing the LLDMS, ERCOT should
therefore set the price‑responsiveness threshold at a level that reflects true emergency conditions.
The threshold should align with circumstances where wholesale energy prices rise to thousands
of dollars per MWh, consistent with conditions that signal a material threat to system reliability
rather than normal market optimization behavior. There should also be a regular screening
process to identify loads that demonstrate price responsive behavior and to disqualify them from
the service.

      4.    How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?

Quantity

When ERCOT develops an event‑specific reliability forecast and estimates hourly probabilities
of load shed based on expected supply and demand conditions, the target procurement quantity
for the LLDMS should be explicitly tied to that forecasted risk. The procured demand reduction
should then be calibrated to reduce the forecasted hourly probabilities of load shed to a de
minimis level.

For example, if ERCOT’s forecast indicates a 5% probability of load shed for some hours for an
upcoming extreme event, the target quantity of load reduction should be the amount necessary to
reduce that probability to a level on the order of 0.1%. In this way, the service would be sized to
address a clearly defined and quantified reliability need, rather than procured on an arbitrary or
fixed basis.

Budget

Establishing the appropriate budget and offer price cap is more complex and should be informed
by empirical data. ERCOT should analyze observed curtailment behavior across different load
types to understand the price levels at which various loads are willing to reduce consumption.
Over time, this analysis should incorporate historical offer data and observed offer curves for
participating loads. Using this information, ERCOT can better determine the budget and price
cap necessary to procure the target quantity of demand reduction while avoiding unnecessary
cost exposure and ensuring that compensation reflects actual willingness to curtail.



PUBLIC                                       5
                             IMM Comments on the Large Load Demand Management Service P-58482
                                                                                April 7, 2026



Auction Structure

We recommend a paid-as-bid auction structure for pricing. The LLDMS product is a short-term
reliability product procured based on anticipated probability of load shed, resulting in a quantity
and budget constraint. It is not intended to provide revenue in a fashion that will incentivize new
investment in load that can participate in this program. As such, the inframarginal rents from a
single-price auction pose an unnecessary cost. While a paid-as-bid auction structure does have
some incentive for participants with lower costs to inflate their offer prices, the fixed
procurement quantity (tied to a budget) does pose risk of unsuccessful offering, so there is a self-
discipling aspect that will keep price inflation in check. One important aspect of this is that offer
prices should not be made public after the auction to prevent future offer inflation.

A paid-as-bid auction also helps reduce potential for the exercise of market power in this case,
since it eliminates the potential for economic withholding on a portion of one’s portfolio to
inflate the price received by the remainder of the portfolio. In the paid-as-bid case, each load can
only be paid the price it offered and will not receive a higher single clearing price.

      5.    What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation
            of PURA § 39.170(b)?

We include most of what we would include here in our General Comments section above
instead.

      6.    PURA §39.170(a) states: The commission shall require the independent organization
            certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure that each
            electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned
            utility serving a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including the
            installation of any necessary equipment or technology before the customer is
            interconnected, to allow the load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric
            cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall
            confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner.
            This subsection applies only to a load interconnected after December 31, 2025, that
            is not: (1) Load operated by a critical load industrial customer, as defined by Section
            17.002; or (2) Designated as a critical natural gas facility under Section 38.074.
            Should the Commission include in this rulemaking a directive implementing PURA
            §39.170(a)?

We recommend such a directive to the extent that critical load industrial customers and critical
natural gas facilities should be excluded from providing the LLDMS.




PUBLIC                                        6
                             IMM Comments on the Large Load Demand Management Service P-58482
                                                                                April 7, 2026



C.    Executive Summary – Potomac Economics – Independent Market Monitor

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the rulemaking for the Large Load Demand
Management Service (LLDMS) organized in Project 58482. We propose the following design
criteria as the foundation of the new service:

     1. Targeted Reliability Tool: We recommend that the PUC adopt Option 1 as described in
     the slides accompanying the initial request for commentary for the LLDMS. This approach
     will allow ERCOT to customize the service in response to an extreme event while
     eliminating costs to load when no such events take place.
     2. Deployed in Response to Real Risk: The conclusion that a given event should be
     classified as extreme and therefore warrant the deployment of the LLDMS should be based
     on a stochastic risk assessment that produces a profile of hourly probabilities of load shed
     that demonstrates a material risk to system reliability for the event period. We note that any
     sensible forecast of Winter Storm Fern, for example, should not have qualified it as an
     extreme event given the extremely low probability of load shed.
     3. Refine Procurement Over Time: The procured quantity for a given extreme event
     should be based on the amount of firm load reduction that would reduce the hourly
     probabilities of load shed to a de minimis amount. To that end, ERCOT should study the
     large load types ahead of the implementation of the LLDMS to understand what budget is
     required to achieve their procurement target given a set of supply and demand conditions.
     Over time, ERCOT should refine this procurement methodology based on the offer behaviors
     of large loads.
     4. Adopt a Robust Set of Eligibility Criteria: Load forecasts for the ERCOT grid predict a
     massive number of large loads to interconnect to ERCOT in the next five years. Given this
     competitive supply, the rulemaking or the stakeholder process should disqualify loads with
     unpredictable baselines, preclude 4CP-responsive loads from participation, and implement a
     process to regularly classify loads as price-responsive to then disqualify them.
     5. Adopt a Paid-As-Bid Auction Structure: In the anticipated competitive participation
     pool, large loads will be incentivized to submit competitive offers to avoid the chance of an
     unsuccessful offer. To avoid gaming future auctions, offer prices should not be made public.
     The potential for exercising market power is also minimized, given that the economic
     withholding of one load in one’s portfolio does not inflate the price received by the rest.

While the above principles constitute an excellent starting point for designing the LLDMS, the
true effectiveness of the new service will depend on its parameters and thresholds. While we
stress that these parameters should arise from empirical data, we also recommend the PUC host a
workshop with stakeholders to explore the following questions:
      •    What magnitude of load shed probability should warrant deploying the LLDMS?
      •    What risk methodology should ERCOT employ to forecast conditions?
      •    How should baselines be established for large loads, and at what point is baseline
           variability too great for a load to participate?
      •    What threshold should be used to determine whether a load is price-responsive?
      •    What should a regular process for classifying loads as price responsive look like?

ECONOMICS
C.    Executive Summary - Potomac Economics - Independent Market Monitor

We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the rulemaking for the Large Load Demand
Management Service (LLDMS) organized in Project 58482. We propose the following design
criteria as the foundation of the new service:

     1. Targeted Reliability Tool: We recommend that the PUC adopt Option 1 as described in
     the slides accompanying the initial request for commentary for the LLDMS. This approach
     will allow ERCOT to customize the service in response to an extreme event while
     eliminating costs to load when no such events take place.
     2. Deployed in Response to Real Risk: The conclusion that a given event should be
     classified as extreme and therefore warrant the deployment of the LLDMS should be based
     on a stochastic risk assessment that produces a profile of hourly probabilities of load shed
     that demonstrates a material risk to system reliability for the event period. We note that any
     sensible forecast of Winter Storm Fern, for example, should not have qualified it as an
     extreme event given the extremely low probability of load shed.
     3. Refine Procurement Over Time: The procured quantity for a given extreme event
     should be based on the amount of firm load reduction that would reduce the hourly
     probabilities of load shed to a de minimis amount. To that end, ERCOT should study the
     large load types ahead of the implementation of the LLDMS to understand what budget is
     required to achieve their procurement target given a set of supply and demand conditions.
     Over time, ERCOT should refine this procurement methodology based on the offer behaviors
     of large loads.
     4. Adopt a Robust Set of Eligibility Criteria: Load forecasts for the ERCOT grid predict a
     massive number of large loads to interconnect to ERCOT in the next five years. Given this
     competitive supply, the rulemaking or the stakeholder process should disqualify loads with
     unpredictable baselines, preclude 4CP-responsive loads from participation, and implement a
     process to regularly classify loads as price-responsive to then disqualify them.
     5. Adopt a Paid-As-Bid Auction Structure: In the anticipated competitive participation
     pool, large loads will be incentivized to submit competitive offers to avoid the chance of an
     unsuccessful offer. To avoid gaming future auctions, offer prices should not be made public.
     The potential for exercising market power is also minimized, given that the economic
     withholding of one load in one' s portfolio does not inflate the price received by the rest.

While the above principles constitute an excellent starting point for designing the LLDMS, the
true effectiveness of the new service will depend on its parameters and thresholds. While we
stress that these parameters should arise from empirical data, we also recommend the PUC host a
workshop with stakeholders to explore the following questions:
       •    What magnitude of load shed probability should warrant deploying the LLDMS?
       •    What risk methodology should ERCOT employ to forecast conditions?
       •    How should baselines be established for large loads, and at what point is baseline
            variability too great for a load to participate?
       •    What threshold should be used to determine whether a load is price-responsive?
       •    What should a regular process for classifying loads as price responsive look like?
